Abstract.

The well-known descent-to-peak map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} for the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions, QSym\mathrm{QSym}, and the peak algebra Π\Pi were originally defined by Stembridge in 1997. We introduce their noncommutative analogues, the labelled descent-to-peak map ΘNCQSym\Theta_{{\mathrm{NCQSym}}} for the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions in noncommuting variables, NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}, and the peak algebra in noncommuting variables NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi. Then, we define the Hopf algebra of Schur QQ-functions in noncommuting variables. We show that our generalizations possess many properties analogous to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we show that the coefficients in the expansion of certain elements of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi in the monomial basis of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} satisfy the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation of Bayer and Billera. In the end, we give representation-theoretic interpretations of the descent-to-peak map for the Hopf algebras of symmetric functions and noncommutative symmetric functions.

Key words and phrases: 
quasisymmetric functions, peak algebra, descent-to-peak map

1. Introduction

The first comprehensive study on the combinatorics of peaks was conducted by Stembridge [44], who developed and introduced enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions, which is an analouge to Stanley’s theory of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions, with the key distinction that the notion of peaks replaces the notion of descents in the context of linear extensions of posets. Generating functions of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions are the fundamental functions, F(P,γ)F_{(P,\gamma)}, which give the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions QSym\mathrm{QSym}, and the generating functions of enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions are the enriched fundamental functions, K(P,γ)K_{(P,\gamma)}, which span the peak algebra Π\Pi. Stembridge also defined the descent-to-peak algebra morphism ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} from QSym\mathrm{QSym} to Π\Pi where F(P,γ)F_{(P,\gamma)} maps to K(P,γ)K_{(P,\gamma)}, and showed that the dimension of the homogenous functions of degree nn of Π\Pi, Πn\Pi_{n}, is equal to the number of odd compositions, compositions whose all parts are odd, which is equal to Fibonacci number fnf_{n}. Moreover, he showed that restricting the map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} to symmetric functions gives the Hopf algebra of Schur QQ-functions. The Hopf algebra of Schur QQ-functions, whose bases are indexed by odd partitions, are introduced in [39] to study the projective representations of symmetric and alternating groups. Combinatorially, the Schur QQ-functions are equipped with a theory of shifted tableaux, including RSK correspondence, Littlewood-Richardson rule, and jeu de taquin [37, 43, 46]. In [12], Bergeron et al. showed that the peak algebra is a Hopf algebra and also the map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} is a Hopf algebra morphism. Also, the main result of [38] by Schocker is that the peak algebra is a left co-ideal of QSym\mathrm{QSym} under internal coproduct.

One intriguing application of peak algebra is its role in providing a combinatorial formula for the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, as discussed. In [19], Brenti and Caselli gave new characterization of the peak subalgebra of the algebra of quasisymmetric functions and used this characterization to construct a new basis for the peak algebra and a combinatorial formula for the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials.

It is also shown that the peak algebra corresponds to the representations of the 00-Hecke-Clifford algebra [14]. Further studies revealed connections between peaks and a variety of seemingly unrelated topics, such as the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation [2, 13, 17] and the Schubert calculus of isotropic flag manifolds [13, 16]. Notably, in [32, 33], the peak algebra is generalized to the Poirier-Reutenauer Hopf algebra of standard Young tableaux, which is introduced in [35]. Other generalizations can be found in [3, 10, 25].

We provide an elegant and natural definition of the peak algebra in noncommuting variables and extend the theta map. We also generalize many known results related to the peak algebra to noncommuting variables. The proofs we provide here differ from the commutative cases; as a result of our constructions, we give alternative and often shorter proofs. Our construction also establishes the definition of Schur QQ-functions in noncommutative variables. We show that the relation between NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi and generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation is the same as that of the commutative case. We also mention two surprising and interesting applications of the internal coproduct of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi given by [47] in the enumeration of Genocchi numbers and qq-tangent numbers, in addition to giving representation-theoretic interpretations of theta maps of symmetric functions and noncommutative symmetric functions.

In Section 2 we provide a summary of the results using generalized chromatic functions along with a compelling combinatorial description of the findings. This section also offers a clear presentation of the results in this paper without proofs, except for the representation-theoretic interpretations. Section 3 gives the relevant background. Section 4 describes set compositions and odd set compositions of [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\} using pairs of subsets of [n−1][n-1] and permutations of [n][n]. In Section 5 we extend the notion of the fundamental functions to noncommuting variables and in Proposition 5.5 prove an analogue of the fundamental theorem of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions. In Section 6 we extend the notion of the enriched fundamental functions to noncommuting variables and in Proposition 6.3 prove an analog of the fundamental theorem of enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions. In Section 7, we introduce enriched monomial functions. In Thereom 7.5, we show that enriched monomial functions give a basis for the peak algebra in noncommuting variables, NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi, and the dimension of the homogenous functions of degree nn of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi, NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}, is equal to the number of odd set compositions, set compositions whose all parts are odd, which is equal to ana_{n} where ana_{n} is the sequence A006154 in the OEIS. In Section 8, we show that NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is a Hopf algebra and describe its product and coproduct in the language of generalized chromatic functions. In Section 9, we extend the notion of descent-to-peak map and define the labelled descent-to-peak map ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}, and give short proofs for the main results in [12]. In Proposition 9.2, we show that ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}} maps the monomial basis of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} to a constant multiple of the enriched monomial basis of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi. In Theorem 9.4, we find the value of ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}} at fundamental functions and that applying the map ρ\rho, where it commutes the variables, we obtain the descent-to-peak map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}. In Section 10, we fix a permutation σn\sigma_{n} in each degree and we show that the coefficients of the expansion of certain elements in NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi in terms of monomial elements 𝐌(A,σn){\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma_{n})} of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} give a function that satisfies the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation. In Section 11, we define the Hopf algebra of Schur QQ-functions in noncommuting variables NC​Ω\mathrm{NC}\Omega and show that it is equal to the restriction of the map ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}} to symmetric functions in noncommuting variables. The Schur QQ-functions that are a basis for NC​Ω\mathrm{NC}\Omega are indexed by odd set partitions. In Section 12 and 13, we present several combinatorial properties of set compositions that we use them in the last section to show that the peak algebra in noncommuting variables is a left co-ideal of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} under internal coproduct, extending Schocker’s result in [39] that the peak algebra is a left co-ideal of QSym\mathrm{QSym} under internal coproduct. In the last section, we present a functor that yields the theta map for the Hopf algebra of symmetric functions. We also provide a representation-theoretic interpretation of the theta map for noncommutative symmetric functions, based on a structure originating from supercharacter theory in Section 14.

2. A painted synopsis

We summarize the combinatorial results of this paper using generalized chromatic functions [5]. For the representation theoretic results see the last section.

2.1. Edge-coloured digraphs and some operators

Stanley [41] defined (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions by generalizing MacMahon’s work on plane partitions [30]11 1 For a complete history of PP-partitions see I. M. Gessel’s paper [23].. (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions can be identified as certain vertex-colourings of some family of edge-coloured digraphs. We describe this family of edge-coloured digraphs and some useful operators between them.

The Hasse diagram of a poset P=(X,≤)P=(X,\leq) can be seen as a digraph whose vertices are the elements of the ground set XX of the poset, and there is a directed edge from aa to bb if a≤ba\leq b and if there is c∈Xc\in X such that a≤c≤ba\leq c\leq b, then either c=ac=a or c=bc=b. Throughout this paper, all digraphs are Hasse diagrams of some posets. For example, the following digraph corresponds to a poset with the ground set {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\}.

An edge-coloured digraph is a digraph whose edges are of the form →\rightarrow or ⇒\Rightarrow.

We now define some useful edge-coloured digraphs. Let QnQ_{n} (resp. PnP_{n}) be the edge-coloured directed path with nn vertices whose all edges are of the form ⇒\Rightarrow (resp. →\rightarrow).

   

The disjoint union of edge-coloured digraphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} with V⁡(G1)∩V⁡(G2)=∅V(G_{1})\cap V(G_{2})=\emptyset, denoted G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}, is an edge-coloured digraph such that

  1. (1)

    The vertex set of G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} is the disjoint union of the vertex sets of G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}.

  2. (2)

    The edge set of G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} is the disjoint union of the edge sets of G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}.

  3. (3)

    a⇒ba\Rightarrow b in G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} if either a⇒ba\Rightarrow b in G1G_{1} or in G2G_{2}.

  4. (4)

    a→ba\rightarrow b in G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} if either a→ba\rightarrow b in G1G_{1} or in G2G_{2}.

The solid sum of edge-coloured directed paths G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, denoted by G1→G2G_{1}\rightarrow G_{2}, is an edge-coloured digraph obtained by connecting the last vertex of G1G_{1} to the first vertex of G2G_{2} by a solid edge →\rightarrow.

2.2. Proper colourings and generalized chromatic functions

As we mentioned earlier, (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions can be identified as certain types of vertex-colourings of edge-coloured digraphs. We describe these types of vertex-colourings of edge-coloured digraphs, and then we construct their generating functions, which are called generalized chromatic functions.

A proper colouring of an edge-coloured digraph GG is a function

κ:V⁡(G)→ℕ={1,2,3,…}\kappa:V(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}

such that

  1. (1)

    If a⇒ba\Rightarrow b, then κ⁡(a)≤κ⁡(b)\kappa(a)\leq\kappa(b).

  2. (2)

    If a→ba\rightarrow b, then κ⁡(a)<κ⁡(b)\kappa(a)<\kappa(b).

Given an edge-coloured digraph, we usually write the colours of the vertices outside of the vertices, which are non-bold positive integers.

Recall that ℚ⁡[[x1,x2,…]]{\mathbb{Q}}[[x_{1},x_{2},\dots]] is the algebra of formal power series in infinitely many commuting variables x={x1,x2,…}x=\{x_{1},x_{2},\dots\} over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

The generalized chromatic function of an edge-coloured digraph GG is

𝒳G=∑κ∏v∈V⁡(G)xκ⁡(v){\mathscr{X}}_{G}=\sum_{\kappa}\prod_{v\in V(G)}x_{\kappa(v)}

where the sum is over all proper colourings κ\kappa of GG. For example, if GG is the edge-coloured digraph in Figure 1, then

Generalized chromatic functions can be seen as generating functions of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions, and so they are quasisymmetric functions (see Section 3.3).

2.3. Enriched colourings and enriched chromatic functions

Stembridge [44] defined enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions and used them to associate tableaux with Schur QQ-functions [39]22 2 For an English reference, see I. G. Macdonald’s book [29, Chapter III, Section 8], where he described Schur’s QQ-functions in more detail. . Enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions can be identified as certain types of vertex-colourings of edge-coloured digraphs. We describe these types of vertex-colourings of edge-coloured digraphs, and then we construct their generating functions, which are called enriched chromatic functions.

Given an edge-coloured digraph GG, an enriched colouring of GG is a function

κ:V(G)→{⋯≺−1≺1≺−2≺2≺⋯}\kappa:V(G)\rightarrow\{\dots\prec-1\prec 1\prec-2\prec 2\prec\cdots\}

such that

  1. (1)

    If a⇒ba\Rightarrow b, then either κ⁡(a)≺κ⁡(b)\kappa(a)\prec\kappa(b) or κ⁡(a)=κ⁡(b)>0\kappa(a)=\kappa(b)>0.

  2. (2)

    If a→ba\rightarrow b, then either κ⁡(a)≺κ⁡(b)\kappa(a)\prec\kappa(b) or κ⁡(a)=κ⁡(b)<0\kappa(a)=\kappa(b)<0.

The enriched chromatic function of an edge-coloured digraph GG is

ℰG=∑κ∏v∈V⁡(G)x|κ⁡(v)|{\mathscr{E}}_{G}=\sum_{\kappa}\prod_{v\in V(G)}x_{|\kappa(v)|}

where the sum is over all enriched colourings κ\kappa of GG. For example, if GG is the edge-coloured digraph in Figure 1, then

2.4. Peak algebra, descent-to-peak map, and earlier results

Stembridge defined the peak algebra Π\Pi33 3 See Section 3.8 for the justification that this space is called the peak algebra. in [44] as a space spanned by the generating functions of enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions. Since generating functions of enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions are the enriched chromatic functions of edge-coloured digraphs and vice versa (Lemma 3.8), we have that the peak algebra is spanned by the set

{ℰG:G is an edge-coloured digraph}.\{{\mathscr{E}}_{G}:\text{$G$ is an edge-coloured digraph}\}.

Stembridge also defined the descent-to-peak map44 4 See Section 3.3 for the justification that this map is called descent-to-peak map. ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}; as shown in Corollary 3.9, we can write it as follows,

ΘQSym:QSym→Π𝒳G↦ℰG.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}:&\mathrm{QSym}&\rightarrow&\Pi\\ &{\mathscr{X}}_{G}&\mapsto&{\mathscr{E}}_{G}.\end{array}

He showed that the descent-to-peak map is a surjective algebra morphism [44, Theorem 3.1].

We now present a series of known results for peak algebra and the descent-to-peak map that we later extend to noncommuting variables.

  1. (1)

    A composition α\alpha of nn, denoted α⊨n\alpha\vDash n, is a list of positive integers whose sum is nn. An odd composition is a composition whose all parts are odd. A set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is called a peak set55 5 The peak set of a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} is the set Peak⁡(σ)={i∈{2,3,…,n−1}:σ⁡(i−1)<σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)}\mathrm{Peak}(\sigma)=\{i\in\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}:\sigma(i-1)<\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}. If i∈Peak⁡(σ)i\in\mathrm{Peak}(\sigma), then i−1,i+1∉Peak⁡(σ)i-1,i+1\not\in\mathrm{Peak}(\sigma). Thus each peak set is the peak set of a permutation. if b∈Bb\in B implies that {b−1,b+1}∩B=∅\{b-1,b+1\}\cap B=\emptyset. By [44, Theorem 3.1] the dimension of the space of the homogeneous elements of degree nn of Π\Pi, Πn\Pi_{n}, is

    dim(Πn)\displaystyle\dim(\Pi_{n}) =|{B⊆{2,3,…,n−1} is a peak set}|\displaystyle=|\{B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}\text{~is a peak set}\}|
    =|{α⊨[n]:α is an odd composition}|\displaystyle=|\{\alpha\vDash[n]:\text{$\alpha$ is an odd composition}\}|
    =fn,\displaystyle=f_{n},

    where fnf_{n} is the nnth Fibonacci number.

  2. (2)

    The peak algebra Π\Pi is a Hopf algebra [12, Theorem 2.2].

  3. (3)

    The descent-to-peak map, ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}, is a Hopf algebra morphism [12, Section 2].

  4. (4)

    The value of the descent-to-peak map at the monomial and fundamental bases elements of QSym\mathrm{QSym} are as follows.

    1. (a)

      Fundamental basis. Given a subset A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1], the fundamental basis element FAF_{A} of QSym\mathrm{QSym} is the generalized chromatic function of the following edge-coloured digraph,

      Qa1→Qa2−a1→…→Qn−ak.Q_{a_{1}}\rightarrow Q_{a_{2}-a_{1}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow Q_{n-a_{k}}.

      Therefore, by the expression of the descent-to-peak map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} in (2.4) we have

      ΘQSym​(FA)=ΘQSym​(𝒳Qa1→Qa2−a1→…→Qn−ak)=ℰQa1→Qa2−a1→…→Qn−ak.\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(F_{A})=\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}({\mathscr{X}}_{Q_{a_{1}}\rightarrow Q_{a_{2}-a_{1}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow Q_{n-a_{k}}})={\mathscr{E}}_{Q_{a_{1}}\rightarrow Q_{a_{2}-a_{1}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow Q_{n-a_{k}}}.
    2. (b)

      Monomial basis. Given a subset A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1], the monomial basis element MAM_{A} of QSym\mathrm{QSym} is

      MA=∑C⊆A(−1)|A|−|C|​FC.M_{A}=\sum_{C\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|C|}F_{C}.

      Given a peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}, the monomial peak function ηB\eta_{B} is

      ηB=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​MA\eta_{B}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}M_{A}

      where

      Odd⁡(B)=[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1)).\mathrm{Odd}(B)=[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1)).

      Let A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1] where n−akn-a_{k} is odd. Then there is a unique peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} such that

      Odd⁡(B)=ODiff⁡(A)\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\mathrm{ODiff}(A)

      where ODiff(A)={ai:1≤i≤k,ai−ai−1 is odd}\mathrm{ODiff}(A)=\{a_{i}:1\leq i\leq k,a_{i}-a_{i-1}\text{ is odd}\} with a0=0a_{0}=0. By [2, Equation (4.9)], we have

      ΘQSym​(MA)\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(M_{A}) ={(−1)n−1−|B|−|A|​ηBif n−max⁡(A) is odd,0otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-1-|B|-|A|}\eta_{B}&\text{if $n-\max(A)$ is odd,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
  5. (5)

    Bayer and Billera [8] generalized the Dehn-Sommerville equation and showed that if a function satisfies this equation, then it is a linear combination of flag ff-vectors of Eulerian posets. Later, in [17], Billera, Hsiao, and van Willigenburg showed that a function ff satisfies the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation if and only if ∑f⁡(A)​MA\sum f(A)M_{A} is in Π\Pi.

  6. (6)

    A partition λ\lambda of nn, denoted λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n, is a non-increasing composition of nn. The values of the descent-to-peak map at different bases of Sym\mathrm{Sym} are as follows.

    1. (a)

      For λ=λ1​λ2​…​λℓ⁡(λ)\lambda=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}\dots\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}, by [5, Table 2] we have that the complete homogeneous symmetric function hλh_{\lambda} (resp., elementary symmetric function eλe_{\lambda}) is the generalized chromatic function of

      OPENQλ=Qλ1⊔Qλ2⊔⋯⊔Qλℓ⁡(λ),(resp.​Pλ=Pλ1⊔Pλ2⊔⋯⊔Pλℓ⁡(λ)).Q_{\lambda}=Q_{\lambda_{1}}\sqcup Q_{\lambda_{2}}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup Q_{\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}},~~~{\text{(resp.}~P_{\lambda}=P_{\lambda_{1}}\sqcup P_{\lambda_{2}}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup P_{\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}})}.

      Thus by the description of the descent-to-peak map in (2.4)

      ΘSym​(hλ)=ℰQλ​(resp. ΘQSym​(eλ)=ℰPλ).\Theta_{\mathrm{Sym}}(h_{\lambda})={\mathscr{E}}_{Q_{\lambda}}~~~\text{(resp. $\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(e_{\lambda})={\mathscr{E}}_{P_{\lambda}}$)}.
    2. (b)

      For λ=λ1λ2⋯λℓ⁡(λ)⊢n\lambda=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}\cdots\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}\vdash n, the Schur function sλs_{\lambda} is

      sλ=det(𝒳Qλi−i+j)1≤i,j≤ℓ⁡(λ).s_{\lambda}=\det\left({\mathscr{X}}_{Q_{\lambda_{i}-i+j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq\ell(\lambda)}.

      By the description of the descent-to-peak map in (2.4)

      ΘSym​(sλ)\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathrm{Sym}}(s_{\lambda}) =ΘSym​(det(𝒳Qλi−i+j)1≤i,j≤ℓ⁡(λ))\displaystyle=\Theta_{\mathrm{Sym}}(\det\left({\mathscr{X}}_{Q_{\lambda_{i}-i+j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq\ell(\lambda)})
      =det(ℰQλi−i+j)1≤i,j≤ℓ⁡(λ).\displaystyle=\det\left({\mathscr{E}}_{Q_{\lambda_{i}-i+j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq\ell(\lambda)}.
    3. (c)

      For λ=λ1​λ2​…​λℓ⁡(λ)⊢n\lambda=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}\dots\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}\vdash n, we have the power sum symmetric function pλp_{\lambda} is

      pλ=(∑i=1xiλ1)(∑i=1xiλ2)⋯(∑i=1xiλℓ⁡(λ)).p_{\lambda}=\left(\sum_{i=1}x_{i}^{\lambda_{1}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}x_{i}^{\lambda_{2}}\right)\cdots\left(\sum_{i=1}x_{i}^{\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)}}\right).

      By [29, Chapter III, Example 10]

      ΘSym​(pλ)={2ℓ⁡(λ)​pλif λ is odd,0otherwise.\Theta_{\mathrm{Sym}}(p_{\lambda})=\begin{cases}2^{\ell(\lambda)}p_{\lambda}&\text{if $\lambda$ is odd,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
  7. (7)

    For a partition λ\lambda, the Schur QQ-function is

    qλ=ℰQλ=ℰPλ.q_{\lambda}={\mathscr{E}}_{Q_{\lambda}}={\mathscr{E}}_{P_{\lambda}}.

    The Hopf algebra of Schur QQ-functions introduced in [39] is denoted by Ω\Omega and

    Ω=ℂ​-span​{qλ:λ​ is an odd partition}.\Omega=\mathbb{C}\text{-span}\{q_{\lambda}:\lambda\text{~is an odd partition}\}.

    Moreover,

    ΘQSym​(Sym)=Ω.\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(\mathrm{Sym})=\Omega.

    By [44, Theorem 3.8], Ω\Omega is the intersection of the Peak algebra Π\Pi and the Hopf algebra of symmetric functions Sym\mathrm{Sym}, that is,

    Ω=Π∩Sym.\Omega=\Pi\cap\mathrm{Sym}.

    The restriction of the descent-to-peak map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} to Sym\mathrm{Sym} is denoted by ΘSym\Theta_{\mathrm{Sym}}. By [44, Theorem 3.1] the following diagram commutes.

  8. (8)

    In [39] Schocker proves that the peak algebra is a left co-ideal of QSym\mathrm{QSym} under internal coproduct.

2.5. Generalized chromatic functions in noncommuting variables

A labelled edge-coloured digraph is an edge-coloured digraph where its vertex set is a subset of ℕ\mathbb{N}. We usually denote the vertices of a labelled edge-coloured digraph by bold positive integers.

We usually use 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} to denote a labelled edge-coloured digraph whose underlying edge-coloured digraph is GG. For example, if we denote the labelled edge-coloured digraph in Figure 3 by 𝐆{\mathbf{G}}, then GG is the edge-coloured digraph in Figure 1.

We now define some useful labelled edge-coloured digraphs. For any set

S={i1<i2<⋯<ik}S=\{i_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k}\}

of positive integers, let QSQ_{S} (resp. PSP_{S}) be the labelled edge-coloured directed path with vertex set SS such that its coloured edges are ij⇒ij+1{i_{j}}\Rightarrow{i_{j+1}} (resp. ij→ij+1{i_{j}}\rightarrow{i_{j+1}}) for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k.

     

The disjoint union of labelled edge-coloured digraphs 𝐆1{\mathbf{G}}_{1} and 𝐆2{\mathbf{G}}_{2} with V⁡(𝐆1)∩V⁡(𝐆2)=∅V({\mathbf{G}}_{1})\cap V({\mathbf{G}}_{2})=\emptyset, is denoted by 𝐆1⊔𝐆2{\mathbf{G}}_{1}\sqcup{\mathbf{G}}_{2}.

The solid sum of labelled edge-coloured directed paths 𝐆1{\mathbf{G}}_{1} and 𝐆2{\mathbf{G}}_{2}, denoted 𝐆1→𝐆2{\mathbf{G}}_{1}\rightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{2}, is an edge-coloured digraph obtained by connecting the last vertex of 𝐆1{\mathbf{G}}_{1} to the first vertex of 𝐆2{\mathbf{G}}_{2} by a solid edge →\rightarrow.

Recall that ℚ⁡⟨⟨𝐱1,𝐱2,…⟩⟩{\mathbb{Q}}\langle\langle{\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2},\dots\rangle\rangle is the algebra of formal power series in infinitely many noncommuting variables 𝐱={𝐱1,𝐱2,…}{\bf x}=\{{\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2},\dots\} over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

The generalized chromatic function in noncommuting variables of a labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} with vertex set [n][n] is

𝒴𝐆=∑κ𝐱κ⁡(1)​𝐱κ⁡(2)​…​𝐱κ⁡(n){\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathbf{G}}=\sum_{\kappa}{\bf x}_{\kappa(1)}{\bf x}_{\kappa(2)}\dots{\bf x}_{\kappa(n)}

where the sum is over all proper colourings κ\kappa of GG. For example, if 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} is the labelled edge-coloured digraph in Figure 3, then

Remark 2.1.

The generalized chromatic functions in noncommuting variables first appeared in [5].

2.6. Enriched chromatic functions in noncommuting variables

The enriched chromatic function in noncommuting variables of a labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} with vertex set [n][n] is

ℱ𝐆=∑κ𝐱|κ⁡(1)|​𝐱|κ⁡(2)|​…​𝐱|κ⁡(n)|{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathbf{G}}=\sum_{\kappa}{\bf x}_{|\kappa(1)|}{\bf x}_{|\kappa(2)|}\dots{\bf x}_{|\kappa(n)|}

where the sum is over all enriched colouring κ\kappa of GG. For example, if 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} is the labelled edge-coloured digraph in Figure 3, then

2.7. Peak algebra in noncommuting variables and labelled descent-to-peak map

In this section, we show that all earlier definitions and results in Section 2.4 can be generalized to noncommuting variables.

The peak algebra in noncommuting variables, denoted NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi, is the space spanned by

{ℱ𝐆:𝐆 is a labelled edge-coloured digraph}.\{{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathbf{G}}:\text{${\mathbf{G}}$ is a labelled edge-coloured digraph}\}.

The labelled descent-to-peak map ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}} is

ΘNCQSym:NCQSym→NC​Π𝒴𝐆↦ℱ𝐆.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}:&\mathrm{NCQSym}&\rightarrow&\mathrm{NC}\Pi\\ &{\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathbf{G}}&\mapsto&{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathbf{G}}.\end{array}
  1. (1)

    A set composition ϕ\phi of [n][n], denoted ϕ⊨[n]\phi\vDash[n], is a sequence of mutually disjoint nonempty sets whose union is [n][n]. An odd set composition is a set composition whose all blocks have odd sizes. We show in Theorem 7.5 that the dimension of the space of homogeneous elements of degree nn of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi, NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}, is

    dim(NC​Πn)\displaystyle\dim(\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}) =|{(B,σ):B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}​ is a peak set and ​Des​(σ)⊆Odd⁡(B)}|\displaystyle=|\{(B,\sigma):B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}\text{~is a peak set and~}\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)\}|
    =|{ϕ⊨[n]:ϕ is an odd set composition}|\displaystyle=|\{\phi\vDash[n]:\text{$\phi$ is an odd set composition}\}|
    =an\displaystyle=a_{n}

    where Des⁡(σ)={i∈[n−1]:σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)},\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)=\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}, and ana_{n} is the sequence A006154 in the OEIS [34].

  2. (2)

    In Section 8, we study the structure of NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi and show that it is a Hopf algebra.

  3. (3)

    In Theorem 9.4, we show that the labelled descent-to-peak map, ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}, is a surjective Hopf algebra morphism and the following diagram commutes.

  4. (4)

    Given a subset A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we say (A,σ)(A,\sigma) is standard if Des⁡(σ)⊆A.\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)\subseteq A. The value of the labelled descent-to-peak map at the monomial and fundamental bases elements of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} are as follows.

    1. (a)

      Fundamental basis. Let A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that (A,σ)(A,\sigma) is standard. The fundamental basis element 𝐅(A,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)} of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} is the generalized chromatic function in noncommuting variables of the following labelled edge-coloured digraph,

      𝐆=Q{σ⁡(1),…,σ⁡(a1)}→Q{σ⁡(a1+1),…,σ⁡(a2)}→…→Q{σ⁡(ak+1),…,σ⁡(n)}.{\mathbf{G}}=Q_{\{\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(a_{1})\}}\rightarrow Q_{\{\sigma(a_{1}+1),\dots,\sigma(a_{2})\}}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow Q_{\{\sigma(a_{k}+1),\dots,\sigma(n)\}}.

      Therefore, by the description of the labelled descent-to-peak map in (2.7)

      ΘNCQSym​(𝐅(A,σ))=ΘNCQSym​(𝒴𝐆)=ℱ𝐆.\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}(\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)})=\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}({\mathscr{Y}}_{{\mathbf{G}}})={\mathscr{F}}_{\mathbf{G}}.
    2. (b)

      Monomial basis. Let A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that (A,σ)(A,\sigma) is standard. The monomial basis element 𝐌(A,σ)\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)} of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} is

      𝐌(A,σ)=∑C⊆A(−1)|A|−|C|​𝐅(C,σ).\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum_{C\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|C|}\mathbf{F}_{(C,\sigma)}.

      For each peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}, the monomial peak function in noncommuting variables 𝜼(B,σ){\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)} is

      𝜼(B,σ)=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}.

      In Proposition 9.2 we show that

      ΘQSym​(𝐌(A,σ))\displaystyle\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}) ={(−1)n−1−|B|−|A|​𝜼(B,σ)if n−max⁡(A) is odd,0otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-1-|B|-|A|}{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}&\text{if $n-\max(A)$ is odd,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
  5. (5)

    If ff is a rational valued function from ⊔n≥0{A:A⊆[n−1]}\sqcup_{n\geq 0}\{A:A\subseteq[n-1]\}, then we define f0​-​1f_{0\text{-}1} to be a rational valued function from the set of 0​-​10\text{-}1 sequences such that f0​-​1(a1a2⋯aℓ(a))=f(A)f_{0\text{-}1}(a_{1}a_{2}\cdots a_{\ell}(a))=f(A) where AA is a subset of [ℓ⁡(a)][\ell(a)] with i∈Ai\in A if and only if ai=1a_{i}=1. In Section 10, we show that the following are equivalent.

    1. (a)

      f0​-​1f_{0\text{-}1} satisfies generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation.

    2. (b)

      f0​-​1f_{0\text{-}1} is a linear combination of flag ff-vectors of Eulerian posets.

    3. (c)

3. Preliminaries

3.1. Compositions

Given a composition α=(α1,α2,…,αk),\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{k}), each αi\alpha_{i} is called a part of α\alpha, the size of α\alpha is |α|=α1+α2+⋯+αk|\alpha|=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\cdots+\alpha_{k}, and the length of α\alpha is kk. By convention, we denote by ∅\emptyset the unique composition of size and length zero. For example, (2,1,2)(2,1,2) is a composition of 55 with length 33.

For every A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\cdots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1], define

Comp⁡(A)=(a1,a2−a1,…,n−ak)⊨[n].{\rm Comp}(A)=(a_{1},a_{2}-a_{1},\dots,n-a_{k})\vDash[n].

For example, if A={2,3}⊆[5]A=\{2,3\}\subseteq[5], then

Comp⁡(A)=(2,1,3).{\rm Comp}(A)=(2,1,3).

The map

{A:A⊆[n−1]}→{α:α⊨[n]}A↦Comp⁡(A)\begin{array}[]{ccc}\{A:A\subseteq[n-1]\}&\rightarrow&\{\alpha:\alpha\vDash[n]\}\\ A&\mapsto&{\rm Comp}(A)\end{array}

is a bijection.

3.2. Odd compositions and peak sets

Recall that an odd composition is a composition whose all parts are odd. We say a subset A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\} of [n−1][n-1] is an odd set if for each 1≤i≤k+11\leq i\leq k+1,

ai−ai−1​ is an odd number,a_{i}-a_{i-1}\text{~is an odd number,}

where a0=0a_{0}=0 and ak+1=n.a_{k+1}=n. Therefore, for any odd set AA, Comp⁡(A){\rm Comp}(A) is an odd composition.

As we mentioned earlier, a set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is called a peak set if b∈Bb\in B implies that {b−1,b+1}∩B=∅\{b-1,b+1\}\cap B=\emptyset. For any peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}, define

Odd⁡(B)=[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1)){\mathrm{Odd}}(B)=[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1))

where B−1={b−1:b∈B}.B-1=\{b-1:b\in B\}. For example, if B={2,5,7,10}⊆{2,3,…,10}B=\{2,5,7,10\}\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,10\}, then

Odd⁡(B)={3,8}.\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\{3,8\}.
Proposition 3.1.

The map

{B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}: B is a peak set}→{A⊆[n−1]: A is an odd set}B↦Odd⁡(B).\begin{array}[]{cccc}\{B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}:\text{~$B$ is a peak set}\}&\rightarrow&\{A\subseteq[n-1]:\text{~$A$ is an odd set}\}\\ B&\mapsto&\mathrm{Odd}(B).\end{array}

is a bijection.

Proof.

Let B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} be a peak set, and let

Odd(B)=[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1))={a1<a2<⋯<ak}.\mathrm{Odd}(B)=[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1))=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\}.

Set a0=0a_{0}=0. Consider that for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, if ai−1≠ai−1a_{i-1}\neq a_{i}-1, then ai−1+1∈(B−1)a_{i-1}+1\in(B-1) and ai−1∈Ba_{i}-1\in B (otherwise, ai−1∈Ba_{i-1}\in B or ai∈Ba_{i}\in B).

Since BB is a peak set, each of BB and B−1B-1 does not include a pair of consecutive integers. Therefore, the sequence

ai−1+1,ai−1+2,…,ai−2,ai−1a_{i-1}+1,a_{i-1}+2,\ldots,a_{i}-2,a_{i}-1

is a sequence whose elements are alternatively in B−1B-1 and BB, that is

ai−1+1∈(B−1),ai−1+2∈B,…,ai−2∈(B−1),ai−1∈B.a_{i-1}+1\in(B-1),a_{i-1}+2\in B,\ldots,a_{i}-2\in(B-1),a_{i}-1\in B.

Therefore, there are an even number of integers between aia_{i} and ai−1a_{i-1}, and so their difference ai−ai−1a_{i}-a_{i-1} is odd. This shows that Odd⁡(B)\mathrm{Odd}(B) is an odd set and the function Odd\mathrm{Odd} is well-defined.

The injectivity of the map Odd\mathrm{Odd} is clear from the definition and now we show that Odd\mathrm{Odd} is bijective. Given an odd set A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1], let

B=⋃i=1k+1{ai−1+2t:t∈ℕ,ai+2t≤ai−1}B=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k+1}\{a_{i-1}+2t:t\in\mathbb{N},a_{i}+2t\leq a_{i}-1\}

where a0=0a_{0}=0 and ak+1=n.a_{k+1}=n. For example, if A={3,8}⊆[10]A=\{3,8\}\subseteq[10], then B={2,5,7,10}.B=\{2,5,7,10\}. We have

Odd⁡(B)=A,\mathrm{Odd}(B)=A,

which gives the inverse of Odd\mathrm{Odd}. ∎

For any peak set BB, define

CompOdd⁡(B)=Comp⁡(Odd⁡(B)).{\rm CompOdd}(B)={\rm Comp}({\rm Odd}(B)).

For example, if B={2,5,7,10}⊆{2,3,…,10}B=\{2,5,7,10\}\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,10\}, then

CompOdd⁡(B)=Comp⁡({3,8})=(3,5,3).{\rm CompOdd}(B)={\rm Comp}(\{3,8\})=(3,5,3).

Since always CompOdd⁡(B){\rm CompOdd}(B) is an odd composition for any peak set BB, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.2.

The map

{B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}: B is a peak set}→{α⊨n: α is odd}B↦CompOdd⁡(B)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\{B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}:\text{~$B$ is a peak set}\}&\rightarrow&\{\alpha\vDash n:\text{~$\alpha$ is odd}\}\\ B&\mapsto&{\rm Comp}\mathrm{Odd}(B)\end{array}

is a bijection.

3.3. PP-partitions, enriched PP-partitions, fundamental functions, and the peak algebra

The notation and definitions in this section mainly follow from [44].

Throughout this paper, P=(X,≤)P=(X,\leq) denotes a partially ordered set of size nn with the ground set XX. A linear extension of PP is a total order w=(w1,w2,…,wn)w=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n}) of the ground set XX such that wi<wjw_{i}<w_{j} implies i<ji<j. The set of linear extensions of PP is denoted by ℒ⁡(P)\mathcal{L}(P). A labelled poset is a pair (P,γ)(P,\gamma) where PP is a poset with ground set XX and γ:X→[n]\gamma:X\to[n] is a bijection.

Let (P,γ)(P,\gamma) be a labelled poset. A (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partition is a map

f:X→ℕ={1,2,3,…}f:X\to\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}

such that for all a,b∈Xa,b\in X with a≤ba\leq b, we have:

  1. (1)

    f⁡(a)≤f⁡(b)f(a)\leq f(b).

  2. (2)

    If γ⁡(a)>γ⁡(b)\gamma(a)>\gamma(b), then f⁡(a)<f⁡(b)f(a)<f(b).

The set of all (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions is denoted by 𝒜⁡(P,γ)\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma).

3.4. Quasisymmetric functions

Given A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1], define the monomial quasisymmetric function MAM_{A} to be

MA=∑xi1α1​xi2α2​…​xikαkM_{A}=\sum x_{i_{1}}^{\alpha_{1}}x_{i_{2}}^{\alpha_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}^{\alpha_{k}}

where (α1,α2,…,αk)=Comp⁡(A)(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{k})={\rm Comp}(A) and the sum is over all tuples (i1,i2,…,ik)(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}) of positive integers such that i1<i2<⋯<iki_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}.

The Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions is

QSym=⨁n≥0QSymn\mathrm{QSym}=\displaystyle\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathrm{QSym}_{n}

where

QSymn=ℚ​-span​{MA:A⊆[n−1]}.\mathrm{QSym}_{n}=\mathbb{Q}\text{-span}\{M_{A}:A\subseteq[n-1]\}.

The basis {MA}\{M_{A}\} is called the monomial basis of the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions.

3.5. Fundamental functions

Given a labelled poset (P,γ)(P,\gamma) with ground set XX, define the fundamental function F(P,γ)F_{(P,\gamma)} to be

F(P,γ)=∑f∈𝒜⁡(P,γ)∏a∈Xxf⁡(a).F_{(P,\gamma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{a\in X}x_{f(a)}.

F_{(P,\gamma)}=&x_{1}x_{2}^{3}&+&x_{1}x_{2}^{2}x_{3}&+&x_{1}x_{2}^{2}x_{3}&+&x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}^{2}&+\cdots.\end{array}

The following is known as the fundamental theorem of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions.

Theorem 3.4.

[42, Lemma 3.15.3] Let (P,γ)(P,\gamma) be a labelled poset. Then

𝒜⁡(P,γ)=⨆w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝒜⁡(w,γ).\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)=\bigsqcup_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma).

Consequently,

F(P,γ)=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)F(w,γ).F_{(P,\gamma)}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}F_{(w,\gamma)}.

Given w=w1​w2​…​wn∈ℒ⁡(P)w=w_{1}w_{2}\dots w_{n}\in\mathcal{L}(P),

Des⁡(w,γ)={i∈{1,2,…,n−1}:γ⁡(wi)>γ⁡(wi+1)}.\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\{i\in\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}:\gamma(w_{i})>\gamma(w_{i+1})\}.

For w∈ℒ⁡(P)w\in\mathcal{L}(P), the function F(w,γ)F_{(w,\gamma)} only depends on the descent set Des⁡(w,γ)\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma) (see [44, Section 2.2]). That is, F(w,γ)=F(w,γ′)F_{(w,\gamma)}=F_{(w,\gamma^{\prime})} if and only if Des⁡(w,γ)=Des⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma^{\prime}). Given A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1], define

FA=F(w,γ)F_{A}=F_{(w,\gamma)}

where (w,γ)(w,\gamma) is any labelled chain with Des⁡(w,γ)=A\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=A.

The set {FA:A⊆[n−1]}\{F_{A}:A\subseteq[n-1]\} is a basis for QSymn\mathrm{QSym}_{n}, and the set {FA}\{F_{A}\} is called the fundamental basis of the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions. We have that

FA=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1]MC.F_{A}=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}M_{C}.
Example 3.5.

Let w=(w1,w2,w3,w4,w5)w=(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4},w_{5}) be a chain, and

γ⁡(w1)​γ​(w2)​γ​(w3)​γ​(w4)​γ​(w5)=34152,\gamma(w_{1})\gamma(w_{2})\gamma(w_{3})\gamma(w_{4})\gamma(w_{5})=34152,

then

Des⁡(w,γ)={2,4},\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\{2,4\},

and so

F{2,4}=F(w,γ).F_{\{2,4\}}=F_{(w,\gamma)}.

Let (P,γ)(P,\gamma) be a labelled poset. An enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partition is a map

f:X→{−1≺1≺−2≺2≺⋯}f:X\to\{-1\prec 1\prec-2\prec 2\prec\cdots\}

such that for all pairs a,b∈Xa,b\in X with a≤ba\leq b, we have:

  1. (1)

    f⁡(a)⪯f⁡(b)f(a)\preceq f(b).

  2. (2)

    f⁡(a)=f⁡(b)>0f(a)=f(b)>0 implies γ⁡(a)<γ⁡(b)\gamma(a)<\gamma(b).

  3. (3)

    f⁡(a)=f⁡(b)<0f(a)=f(b)<0 implies γ⁡(a)>γ⁡(b)\gamma(a)>\gamma(b).

The set of all enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions is denoted by ℬ⁡(P,γ)\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma).

Given a labelled poset (P,γ)(P,\gamma) with ground set XX, define the enriched fundamental function K(P,γ)K_{(P,\gamma)} to be

K(P,γ)=∑f∈ℬ⁡(P,γ)∏a∈Xx|f⁡(a)|.K_{(P,\gamma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{a\in X}x_{|f(a)|}.

K_{(P,\gamma)}=&x_{1}^{4}&+&x_{1}^{4}&+&x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{2}&+&x_{1}x_{2}^{3}&+\cdots.\end{array}

The following is the analogue of the fundamental theorem for enriched PP-partitions.

Theorem 3.7.

[44, Lemma 2.1] Let (P,γ)(P,\gamma) be a labelled poset. Then

ℬ⁡(P,γ)=⨆w∈ℒ⁡(P)ℬ⁡(w,γ).\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)=\bigsqcup_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma).

Consequently,

K(P,γ)=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)K(w,γ).K_{(P,\gamma)}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}K_{(w,\gamma)}.

Given w∈ℒ⁡(P)w\in\mathcal{L}(P),

Peak⁡(w,γ)={i:γ⁡(wi−1)<γ⁡(wi)>γ⁡(wi+1)}\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)=\{i:\gamma(w_{i-1})<\gamma(w_{i})>\gamma(w_{i+1})\}

is a peak set, and also any peak set is equal to some Peak⁡(w,γ)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma).

For w∈ℒ⁡(P)w\in\mathcal{L}(P), the function K(w,γ)K_{(w,\gamma)} only depends on the peak set Peak⁡(w,γ)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma) (see [44, Section 2.2]). That is, K(w,γ)=K(w,γ′)K_{(w,\gamma)}=K_{(w,\gamma^{\prime})} if and only if Peak⁡(w,γ)=Peak⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma^{\prime}). Given a peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}, define

KB=K(w,γ)K_{B}=K_{(w,\gamma)}

where (w,γ)(w,\gamma) is any labelled chain with Peak⁡(w,γ)=B\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)=B.

The peak algebra is

Π=⨁n≥0Πn\Pi=\displaystyle\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\Pi_{n}

where

Πn=ℚ​-span​{KB:B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}​ is a peak set}.\Pi_{n}={\mathbb{Q}}\text{-span}\{K_{B}:B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}\text{~is a peak set}\}.

The basis {KB:B​ is a peak set}\{K_{B}:B\text{~is a peak set}\} is called the enriched fundamental basis of the peak algebra.

Given a peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}, define the enriched monomial function to be

ηB=∑C⊆B(−1)|B|−|C|​KC.\eta_{B}=\sum_{C\subseteq B}(-1)^{|B|-|C|}K_{C}.

By inclusion-exclusion, we have

KB=∑C⊆BηC.K_{B}=\sum_{C\subseteq B}\eta_{C}.

The descent-to-peak map is

ΘQSym:QSym→ΠF(P,γ)↦K(P,γ),\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}:&\mathrm{QSym}&\to&\Pi\\ &F_{(P,\gamma)}&\mapsto&K_{(P,\gamma)},\end{array}

which is a surjective morphism of graded Hopf algebras (see [12]).

When (w,γ)(w,\gamma) is a labelled chain with descent set AA and peak set BB, then

ΘQSym​(FA)=ΘQSym​(F(w,γ))=K(w,γ)=KB,\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(F_{A})=\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}(F_{(w,\gamma)})=K_{(w,\gamma)}=K_{B},

so ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} maps a fundamental basis element indexed by a descent set of a labelled chain to the enriched fundamental basis element indexed by the peak set of the same labelled chain. Consequently, the map ΘQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}} is called the descent-to-peak map.

Lemma 3.8.

Given a labelled poset (P,γ)(P,\gamma), let GG be an edge-coloured digraph isomorphic to the Hasse diagram of PP, and moreover,

  1. (1)

    a⇒ba\Rightarrow b in GG if and and only if bb covers aa in PP and γ⁡(a)≤γ⁡(b)\gamma(a)\leq\gamma(b).

  2. (2)

    a→ba\rightarrow b in GG if and and only if bb covers aa in PP and γ⁡(a)>γ⁡(b)\gamma(a)>\gamma(b).

Then

  1. (i)

    the set of (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions and the set of proper colourings of GG are identical,

  2. (ii)

    F(P,γ)=𝒳G,F_{(P,\gamma)}={\mathscr{X}}_{G},

  3. (iii)

    the set of enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions and the set of enriched colourings of GG are identical,

  4. (iv)

    K(P,γ)=ℰG.K_{(P,\gamma)}={\mathscr{E}}_{G}.

The above lemma enables us to translate the results about (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partitions and peak algebra into the language of generalized chromatic functions.

Corollary 3.9.

The descent-to-peak map can be rewritten as

ΘQSym:QSym→Π𝒳G↦ℰG.\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Theta_{\mathrm{QSym}}:&\mathrm{QSym}&\to&\Pi\\ &{\mathscr{X}}_{G}&\mapsto&{\mathscr{E}}_{G}.\end{array}

4. Standard and enriched standard pairs

4.1. Set compositions and standard pairs

Recall that a set composition ϕ\phi of [n][n] is a list of mutually disjoint nonempty subsets ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕℓ⁡(ϕ)\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\ldots,\phi_{\ell(\phi)} of [n][n] whose union is [n][n]; this is denoted by ϕ1|ϕ2|⋯|ϕℓ⁡(ϕ)⊨[n]\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}|\cdots|\phi_{\ell(\phi)}\vDash[n]. Each ϕi\phi_{i} is called a block of the set composition ϕ\phi, and the length of ϕ\phi is ℓ⁡(ϕ)\ell(\phi). By convention, we denote by ∅\emptyset the unique empty set composition of [0]=∅[0]=\emptyset. For example, ϕ=12​|5|​34⊨[5]\phi=12|5|34\vDash[5] has length 3.

Given a pair (A,σ)(A,\sigma), A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, define

SetComp(A,σ)=σ(1)⋯σ(a1)|σ(a1+1)⋯σ(a2)|⋯|σ(ak)⋯σ(n)⊨[n].\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)=\sigma(1)\cdots\sigma(a_{1})~|~\sigma(a_{1}+1)\cdots\sigma(a_{2})~|\cdots|~\sigma(a_{k})\cdots\sigma(n)\vDash[n].

For example,

SetComp⁡({2,5,6},67325841)=67|325​|8|​41.\mathrm{SetComp}(\{2,5,6\},67325841)=67|325|8|41.

Let A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Remember that the pair (A,σ)(A,\sigma) is standard if Des⁡(σ)⊆A\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)\subseteq A, that is a∉Aa\notin A implies σ⁡(a)<σ⁡(a+1)\sigma(a)<\sigma(a+1). For example, when A={2,5,6}A=\{2,5,6\} and σ=37124856\sigma=37124856, then (A,σ)(A,\sigma) is standard and SetComp⁡(A,σ)=37|124​|8|​56\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)=37|124|8|56. Note that for any pair (A,σ)(A,\sigma), A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, there is a unique σ′∈𝔖n\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that (A,σ′)(A,\sigma^{\prime}) is standard and SetComp⁡(A,σ)=SetComp⁡(A,σ′)\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)=\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma^{\prime}). We denote (A,σ′)(A,\sigma^{\prime}) by Std⁡(A,σ)\mathrm{Std}(A,\sigma). For example,

Std⁡({3,5},37284516)=({3,5},23748156).\mathrm{Std}(\{3,5\},37284516)=(\{3,5\},23748156).
Proposition 4.1.

The map

{(A,σ):A⊆[n−1],σ∈𝔖n,(A,σ)isstandard}→{ϕ:ϕ⊨[n]}(A,σ)↦SetComp⁡(A,σ)\begin{array}[]{cccc}&\{(A,\sigma):A\subseteq[n-1],\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n},(A,\sigma)~{\rm is~standard}\}&\rightarrow&\{\phi:\phi\vDash[n]\}\\ &(A,\sigma)&\mapsto&\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)\end{array}

is a bijection.

Proof.

We first show that the function SetComp\mathrm{SetComp} is surjective. Given a set composition ϕ=ϕ1|ϕ2​|…|​ϕℓ⁡(ϕ)\phi=\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}|\dots|\phi_{\ell(\phi)}, let ϕi​j\phi_{ij} be the jjth smallest element in ϕi\phi_{i}. Let k=ℓ⁡(ϕ)−1k=\ell(\phi)-1. Let |ϕi|=ai−ai−1|\phi_{i}|=a_{i}-a_{i-1}, 1≤i≤k+11\leq i\leq k+1, with a0=0a_{0}=0 and ak+1=na_{k+1}=n. Set

σ=ϕ11​ϕ12​…​ϕ1​a1​ϕ21​ϕ22​…​ϕ2​(a2−a1)​…​ϕk​1​ϕk​2​…​ϕk⁡(n−ak)\sigma=\phi_{11}\phi_{12}\dots\phi_{1a_{1}}\phi_{21}\phi_{22}\dots\phi_{2(a_{2}-a_{1})}\dots\phi_{k1}\phi_{k2}\dots\phi_{k(n-a_{k})}

and

A={a1,a2,…,ak}A=\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}\}

then

SetComp⁡(A,σ)=ϕ11​ϕ12​…​ϕ1​a1​|ϕ21​ϕ22​…​ϕ2​(a2−a1)|​…|ϕk​1​ϕk​2​…​ϕk⁡(n−ak)=ϕ.\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)=\phi_{11}\phi_{12}\dots\phi_{1a_{1}}~|~\phi_{21}\phi_{22}\dots\phi_{2(a_{2}-a_{1})}~|\dots|~\phi_{k1}\phi_{k2}\dots\phi_{k(n-a_{k})}=\phi.

Therefore, the function SetComp\mathrm{SetComp} is surjective.

Now we show that SetComp\mathrm{SetComp} is an injection. If ϕ=SetComp⁡(A,σ)=SetComp⁡(A′,σ′)\phi=\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)=\mathrm{SetComp}(A^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}), since AA and A′A^{\prime} identify the sizes of the blocks of ϕ\phi, we have that A=A′A=A^{\prime}. Moreover, by the definition of the function SetComp\mathrm{SetComp}, we must have σ=σ′\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}. Therefore, SetComp\mathrm{SetComp} is injective.

∎

4.2. Odd set compositions and enriched standard pairs

An odd set composition is a set composition whose all blocks have odd sizes. We say a pair (A,σ)(A,\sigma), A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, is odd if AA is an odd set. Therefore, for any odd pair (A,σ)(A,\sigma), SetComp⁡(A,σ){\rm SetComp}(A,\sigma) is an odd set composition.

A pair (B,σ)(B,\sigma), B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, is called enriched standard if (Odd⁡(B),σ)(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma) is standard, that is Des⁡(σ)⊆Odd⁡(B)\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B). For example, when B={2,5,7}B=\{2,5,7\} and σ=278134569\sigma=278134569, then (B,σ)(B,\sigma) is enriched standard since

Des⁡(σ)={3}⊆Odd⁡(B)={3,8}.\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)=\{3\}\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\{3,8\}.

Note that for any pair (B,σ)(B,\sigma), B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, there is a unique σ′∈𝔖n\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that (B,σ′)(B,\sigma^{\prime}) is enriched standard. We denote (B,σ′)(B,\sigma^{\prime}) by EStd⁡(B,σ){\rm EStd}(B,\sigma). For example,

EStd⁡({2,5,7},287134659)=({2,5,7},278134569).{\rm EStd}(\{2,5,7\},287134659)=(\{2,5,7\},278134569).

For each enriched standard pair (B,σ)(B,\sigma), define

SetCompOdd⁡(B,σ)=SetComp⁡(Odd⁡(B),σ).\mathrm{SetCompOdd}(B,\sigma)=\mathrm{SetComp}(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma).
Proposition 4.2.

The map from the set of enriched standard pairs (B,σ)(B,\sigma), B⊆[n−1]B\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, to the set of odd set compositions of [n][n] given by

(B,σ)↦SetCompOdd⁡(B,σ).\begin{array}[]{cccc}&(B,\sigma)&\mapsto&\mathrm{SetCompOdd}(B,\sigma).\end{array}

is a bijection.

Proof.

To show that SetCompOdd\mathrm{SetCompOdd} is a bijection, we only need to show that it is surjective. Given an odd set composition

ϕ=ϕ1|ϕ2​|⋯|​ϕℓ⁡(ϕ),\phi=\phi_{1}|\phi_{2}|\cdots|\phi_{\ell(\phi)},

let BB be a peak set such that

Odd(B)={|ϕ1|<|ϕ1|+|ϕ2|<⋯<|ϕ1|+|ϕ2|+⋯+|ϕℓ⁡(ϕ)−1|},\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\{|\phi_{1}|<|\phi_{1}|+|\phi_{2}|<\cdots<|\phi_{1}|+|\phi_{2}|+\cdots+|\phi_{\ell(\phi)-1}|\},

and let σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} be the permutation for which

σ({|ϕ1|+⋯+|ϕi−1|+1,|ϕ1|+⋯+|ϕi−1|+2,|ϕ1|+⋯+|ϕi−1|+|ϕi|)=sort(ϕi)\sigma(\{|\phi_{1}|+\cdots+|\phi_{i-1}|+1,|\phi_{1}|+\cdots+|\phi_{i-1}|+2,|\phi_{1}|+\cdots+|\phi_{i-1}|+|\phi_{i}|)={\mathrm{sort}}(\phi_{i})

for all ii. Then

SetCompOdd⁡(B,σ)=ϕ.\mathrm{SetCompOdd}(B,\sigma)=\phi.

∎

5. Fundamental functions in noncommuting variables and the analogue of the fundamental theorem

5.1. Quasisymmetric functions in noncommuting variables

Recall that ℚ⁡⟨⟨𝐱1,𝐱2,…⟩⟩{\mathbb{Q}}\langle\langle{\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2},\dots\rangle\rangle is the algebra of formal power series in infinitely many noncommuting variables 𝐱={𝐱1,𝐱2,…}{\bf x}=\{{\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2},\dots\} over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}.

Given (A,σ)(A,\sigma), A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, define the monomial quasisymmetric function in noncommuting variables 𝐌(A,σ){\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma)} to be

𝐌(A,σ)=∑𝐱i1𝐱i2⋯𝐱in{\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum{\bf x}_{i_{1}}{\bf x}_{i_{2}}\cdots{\bf x}_{i_{n}}

where the sum is over all tuples (i1,i2,…,in)(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{n}) of positive integers such that

  1. (1)

    ij=iki_{j}=i_{k} if and only if jj and kk are in the same block of SetComp⁡(A,σ)\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma).

  2. (2)

    ij<iki_{j}<i_{k} if and only if jj is in a block of SetComp⁡(A,σ)\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma) to the left of the block containing kk.

Note that for pairs (A,σ1)(A,\sigma_{1}) and (A,σ2)(A,\sigma_{2}) with Std⁡(A,σ1)=Std⁡(A,σ2)\mathrm{Std}(A,\sigma_{1})=\mathrm{Std}(A,\sigma_{2}), we have

𝐌(A,σ1)=𝐌(A,σ2).\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma_{1})}=\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma_{2})}.

The Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions in noncommuting variables is

NCQSym=⨁n≥0NCQSymn\mathrm{NCQSym}=\displaystyle\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathrm{NCQSym}_{n}

where

NCQSymn=ℚ-span{𝐌(A,σ):A⊆[n−1],σ∈𝔖n, (A,σ) is standard}.\mathrm{NCQSym}_{n}=\mathbb{Q}\text{-span}\{\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}:A\subseteq[n-1],\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},\text{~$(A,\sigma)$ is standard}\}.

The basis {𝐌(A,σ):(A,σ) is standard}\{\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}:\text{$(A,\sigma)$ is standard}\} is called the monomial basis of the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions in noncommuting variables.

5.2. Fundamental functions in noncommuting variables

Given (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma) where (P,γ)(P,\gamma) is a labelled poset with ground set XX, |X|=n|X|=n, and σ:X→[n]\sigma:X\to[n] is a bijection, define the fundamental function in noncommuting variables 𝐅(P,γ,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)} to be

𝐅(P,γ,σ)=∑f∈𝒜⁡(P,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i))=∑f∈𝒜⁡(P,γ)𝐱f​(σ−1​(1))𝐱f​(σ−1​(2))⋯𝐱f​(σ−1​(n)).\mathbf{F}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(2))}\cdots\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(n))}.

Definition 5.2.

Let (P,γ)(P,\gamma) be a labelled poset with ground set XX and |X|=n|X|=n. Let σ:X→[n]\sigma:X\to[n] be a bijection. The labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} associated to (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma) is a labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} such that

  1. (1)

    The vertex set of 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} is [n][n].

  2. (2)

    σ−1​(a)⇒σ−1​(b)\sigma^{-1}(a)\Rightarrow\sigma^{-1}(b) in 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} if and only if bb covers aa in PP and γ⁡(σ−1​(a))<γ⁡(σ−1​(b))\gamma(\sigma^{-1}(a))<\gamma(\sigma^{-1}(b)).

  3. (3)

    σ−1​(a)→σ−1​(b)\sigma^{-1}(a)\rightarrow\sigma^{-1}(b) in 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} if and only if bb covers aa in PP and γ⁡(σ−1​(a))>γ⁡(σ−1​(b))\gamma(\sigma^{-1}(a))>\gamma(\sigma^{-1}(b)).

Lemma 5.3.

Given the labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} associated to (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma), we have

𝐅(P,γ,σ)=𝒴𝐆.{\mathbf{F}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}={\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathbf{G}}.
Example 5.4.

Given (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma) in Example 5.1,

𝐅(P,γ,σ)=𝒴𝐆{\mathbf{F}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}={\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathbf{G}}

where 𝐆{\mathbf{G}} is the following edge-coloured digraph.

5.3. The analogue of the fundamental theorem

From now on w=(w1,w2,…,wn)w=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n}) is a chain with the ground set {w1,w2,…,wn}={1,2,…,n}\{w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n}\}=\{1,2,\dots,n\}. So we can look at any bijection σ:{w1,w2,…,wn}→[n]\sigma:\{w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n}\}\rightarrow[n] as a permutation in 𝔖n{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}.

Proposition 5.5.

We have that

𝐅(P,γ,σ)=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝐅(w,γ,σ).\mathbf{F}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}.
Proof.

By Theorem 3.4, we have 𝒜⁡(P,γ)=⨆w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝒜⁡(w,γ)\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)=\bigsqcup_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma). Hence,

𝐅(P,γ,σ)=∑f∈𝒜⁡(P,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i))=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)(∑f∈𝒜⁡(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i)))=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝐅(w,γ,σ).\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}\right)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}.

∎

Proposition 5.6.

We have that 𝐅(w,γ,σ)=𝐅(w,γ′,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma^{\prime},\sigma)} if and only if Des⁡(w,γ)=Des⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma^{\prime}).

Proof.

If Des⁡(w,γ)=Des⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma^{\prime}), by definition, f∈𝒜⁡(w,γ)f\in\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma) implies f∈𝒜⁡(w,γ′)f\in\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma^{\prime}). Therefore, 𝐅(w,γ,σ)=𝐅(w,γ′,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma^{\prime},\sigma)}.

Conversely, if 𝐅(w,γ,σ)=𝐅(w,γ′,σ){\mathbf{F}}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}={\mathbf{F}}_{(w,\gamma^{\prime},\sigma)}, then commuting the variables we have F(w,γ)=F(w,γ)F_{(w,\gamma)}=F_{(w,\gamma)}. Therefore, Des⁡(w,γ)=Des⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma^{\prime}). ∎

Given A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, define

𝐅(A,σ)=𝐅(w,γ,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}

where (w,γ)(w,\gamma) is any labelled chain with Des⁡(w,γ)=A\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=A.

Example 5.7.

Let w=(w1,w2,w3,w4,w5)w=(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4},w_{5}) be a chain,

γ⁡(w1)​γ​(w2)​γ​(w3)​γ​(w4)​γ​(w5)=34152,\gamma(w_{1})\gamma(w_{2})\gamma(w_{3})\gamma(w_{4})\gamma(w_{5})=34152,

and

σ⁡(w1)​σ​(w2)​σ​(w3)​σ​(w4)​σ​(w5)=51423,\sigma(w_{1})\sigma(w_{2})\sigma(w_{3})\sigma(w_{4})\sigma(w_{5})=51423,

then

Des⁡(w,γ)={2,4},\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=\{2,4\},

and so

𝐅({2,4},σ)=𝐅(w,γ,σ).{\mathbf{F}}_{(\{2,4\},\sigma)}={\mathbf{F}}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}.

5.4. Fundamental functions to monomial basis

Proposition 5.8.

Let A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Then

𝐅(A,σ)=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1]𝐌(C,σ).\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\mathbf{M}_{(C,\sigma)}.
Proof.

By definition, 𝐅(A,σ)=𝐅(w,γ,σ)\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\mathbf{F}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)} where w=(1,2,…,n)w=(1,2,\dots,n) and Des⁡(w,γ)=A\mathrm{Des}(w,\gamma)=A. Note the set of (w,γ)(w,\gamma)-partitions, 𝒜⁡(w,γ)\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma), can be decomposed into

𝒜⁡(w,γ)=⨆A⊆C⊆[n−1]𝒜C​(w,γ),\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma)=\bigsqcup_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\mathcal{A}_{C}(w,\gamma),

where 𝒜C​(w,γ)\mathcal{A}_{C}(w,\gamma) is the set of (w,γ)(w,\gamma)-partitions ff such that f⁡(wi)<f⁡(wi+1)f(w_{i})<f(w_{i+1}) if and only if i∈Ci\in C. Therefore,

𝐅(A,σ)=∑f∈𝒜⁡(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i))=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](∑f∈𝒜C​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i))).\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}_{C}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}\right).

For each A⊆C⊆[n−1]A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1], we have

∑f∈𝒜C​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i))=𝐌(C,σ).\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}_{C}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}=\mathbf{M}_{(C,\sigma)}.

Therefore,

𝐅(A,σ)=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](∑f∈𝒜C​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱f​(σ−1​(i)))=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1]𝐌(C,σ).\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{A}_{C}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{f(\sigma^{-1}(i))}\right)=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\mathbf{M}_{(C,\sigma)}.

∎

Corollary 5.9.

The set {𝐅(A,σ):(A,σ)​ is standard}\{\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}:(A,\sigma)\text{ is standard}\} forms a basis of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.1 we have

𝐅(A,σ)=∑A⊆C⊆[n−1]𝐌(C,σ).\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}=\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}\mathbf{M}_{(C,\sigma)}.

Note that A⊆CA\subseteq C if and only if SetComp⁡(A,σ)≤SetComp⁡(C,σ)\mathrm{SetComp}(A,\sigma)\leq\mathrm{SetComp}(C,\sigma). The result follows from triangularity and Proposition 4.1. ∎

We call {𝐅(A,σ):(A,σ)​ is standard}\{\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}:(A,\sigma)\text{ is standard}\} the fundamental basis of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}.

Remark 5.10.

The fundamental basis also appears in [5, Section 11].

6. Enriched fundamental functions in noncommuting variables and the analogue of the fundamental theorem

6.1. Enriched fundamental functions in noncommuting variables

In this section, we present the enriched fundamental functions in noncommuting variables.

Given (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma) where (P,γ)(P,\gamma) is a labelled poset with ground set XX, |X|=n|X|=n, and σ:X→[n]\sigma:X\to[n] is a bijection, define the enriched fundamental function in noncommuting variables 𝐊(P,γ,σ)\mathbf{K}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)} to be

𝐊(P,γ,σ)=∑f∈ℬ⁡(P,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|=∑f∈ℬ⁡(P,γ)𝐱|f​(σ−1​(1))|​𝐱|f​(σ−1​(2))|​…​𝐱|f​(σ−1​(n))|.\mathbf{K}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(1))|}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(2))|}\dots\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(n))|}.

Lemma 6.2.

Given the labelled edge-coloured digraph 𝐆{\bf G} associated to (P,γ,σ)(P,\gamma,\sigma), we have

𝐊(P,γ,σ)=ℱ𝐆.{\mathbf{K}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}={\mathscr{F}}_{\bf G}.

6.2. The analogue of the fundamental theorem

Proposition 6.3.

We have that

𝐊(P,γ,σ)=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝐊(w,γ,σ).\mathbf{K}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}.
Proof.

By Theorem 3.7, we have ℬ⁡(P,γ)=⨆w∈ℒ⁡(P)ℬ⁡(w,γ)\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)=\bigsqcup_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma). Hence,

𝐊(P,γ,σ)=∑f∈ℬ⁡(P,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)(∑f∈ℬ⁡(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|)=∑w∈ℒ⁡(P)𝐊(w,γ,σ).\displaystyle\mathbf{K}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(P,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}\right)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{L}(P)}\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}.

∎

6.3. Enriched fundamental functions to monomial basis

First, we expand the 𝐊\mathbf{K} functions in the 𝐌\mathbf{M} basis, showing that NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is a subspace of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}. The idea of the proof is similar to the commutative case given in [44].

Proposition 6.4.

Assume w=(w1,w2,…,wn)w=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n}) is a chain and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we have

𝐊(w,γ,σ)=∑A⊆[n−1]Peak⁡(w,γ)⊆A∪(A+1)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]\atop\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\subseteq A\cup(A+1)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}.
Proof.

Recall that

𝐊(w,γ,σ)=∑f∈ℬ⁡(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|.{\mathbf{K}}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}.

Fix A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1] with 0=a00=a_{0} and ak+1=na_{k+1}=n. Define

[A]=12…a1|(a1+1)(a1+2)…a2|⋯|(ak+1)(ak+2)⋯an.[A]=12\dots a_{1}~|~(a_{1}+1)(a_{1}+2)\dots a_{2}~|\cdots|(a_{k}+1)(a_{k}+2)\cdots a_{n}.

Let

ℬA​(w,γ)\mathcal{B}_{A}(w,\gamma)

be the set of all f∈ℬ⁡(w,γ)f\in\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma) such that

  1. (1)

    |f⁡(wi)|=|f⁡(wj)||f(w_{i})|=|f(w_{j})| if ii and jj are in the same block of [A][A].

  2. (2)

    |f⁡(wi)|<|f⁡(wj)||f(w_{i})|<|f(w_{j})| if ii is in a block of [A][A] to the left of the block containing jj.

Then

𝐊(w,γ,σ)=∑f∈ℬ⁡(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|=∑A⊆[n−1](∑f∈ℬA​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|).{\mathbf{K}}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}=\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}_{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}\right).

We will show the following claims are true.

  • (I)

    If Peak⁡(w,γ)⊈A∪(A+1)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\not\subseteq A\cup(A+1), then ℬA​(w,γ){\mathcal{B}}_{A}(w,\gamma) is empty.

  • (II)

    If Peak⁡(w,γ)⊆A∪(A+1)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\subseteq A\cup(A+1), then

    ∑f∈ℬA​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|=2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}_{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}=2^{|A|+1}{\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma)}.

Therefore,

𝐊(w,γ,σ)=∑A⊆[n−1](∑f∈ℬA​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|)=∑A⊆[n−1]Peak⁡(w,γ)⊆A∪(A+1)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ),{\mathbf{K}}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}_{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}\right)=\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]\atop\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\subseteq A\cup(A+1)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)},

as desired.

Proof of (I). Let b∈Peak⁡(w,γ)∖A∪(A+1)b\in\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\setminus A\cup(A+1). Since

Peak⁡(w,γ)∖A∪(A+1)⊆{2,3,…,n−1}∖A∪(A+1)=\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\setminus A\cup(A+1)\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}\setminus A\cup(A+1)=
{2,3,…,a1−1,a1+2,a1+3,…,a2−1,…,ak+2,ak+3,…,n},\{2,3,\dots,a_{1}-1,a_{1}+2,a_{1}+3,\dots,a_{2}-1,\dots,a_{k}+2,a_{k}+3,\dots,n\},

we have that b−1,b,b+1b-1,b,b+1 are in the same block of [A][A]. Therefore, if f∈ℬA​(w,γ)≠∅f\in{\mathcal{B}}_{A}(w,\gamma)\neq\emptyset, we must have

|f⁡(wb−1)|=|f⁡(wb)|=|f⁡(wb+1)|.|f(w_{b-1})|=|f(w_{b})|=|f(w_{b+1})|.

Note that bb is in Peak⁡(w,γ)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma), and so

γ⁡(wb−1)<γ⁡(wb)>γ⁡(wb+1).\gamma(w_{b-1})<\gamma(w_{b})>\gamma(w_{b+1}).

Since ff is an enriched (P,γ)(P,\gamma)-partition,

f⁡(wb−1)⪯f⁡(wb)⪯f⁡(wb+1).f(w_{b-1})\preceq f(w_{b})\preceq f(w_{b+1}).

If |f⁡(wb−1)|=|f⁡(wb)||f(w_{b-1})|=|f(w_{b})| then f⁡(wb−1)=f⁡(b)>0f(w_{b-1})=f(b)>0, and if |f⁡(wb)|=|f⁡(wb+1)||f(w_{b})|=|f(w_{b+1})| then f⁡(wb−1)=f⁡(b)<0f(w_{b-1})=f(b)<0. Therefore, we can not have |f⁡(wb−1)|=|f⁡(wb)|=|f⁡(wb+1)|,|f(w_{b-1})|=|f(w_{b})|=|f(w_{b+1})|, a contradiction. Therefore, ℬA​(w,γ)=∅{\mathcal{B}}_{A}(w,\gamma)=\emptyset.

Proof of (II). If Peak⁡(w,γ)⊆A∪(A+1)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)\subseteq A\cup(A+1), then for each 1≤j≤ℓ−11\leq j\leq\ell-1, we have

γ⁡(waj+1)≤γ⁡(waj+2)≤⋯≤γ⁡(waj+t)≥⋯≥γ⁡(waj+1−1)≥γ⁡(waj+1)\gamma(w_{a_{j}+1})\leq\gamma(w_{a_{j}+2})\leq\dots\leq\gamma(w_{a_{j}+t})\geq\dots\geq\gamma(w_{a_{j+1}-1})\geq\gamma(w_{a_{j+1}})

(note that we may have t=1t=1 or t=(aj+1−aj)t=(a_{j+1}-a_{j}), which in these cases γ\gamma is decreasing or increasing, respectively). Then there are two types of f∈ℬA​(P,γ)f\in{\mathcal{B}}_{A}(P,\gamma):

  • •

    f⁡(waj+t)<0f(w_{a_{j}+t})<0, f⁡(waj+t)=f⁡(waj+s)f(w_{a_{j}+t})=f(w_{a_{j}+s}) for 1≤s≤t1\leq s\leq t, and f⁡(waj+t)=−f⁡(waj+s)f(w_{a_{j}+t})=-f(w_{a_{j}+s}) for t+1≤s≤aj+1−ajt+1\leq s\leq a_{j+1}-a_{j}.

  • •

    f⁡(waj+t)>0f(w_{a_{j}+t})>0, f⁡(waj+t)=f⁡(waj+s)f(w_{a_{j}+t})=f(w_{a_{j}+s}) for 1≤s≤t1\leq s\leq t, and f⁡(waj+t)=−f⁡(waj+s)f(w_{a_{j}+t})=-f(w_{a_{j}+s}) for t+1≤s≤aj+1−ajt+1\leq s\leq a_{j+1}-a_{j}.

Therefore, there are 2|A|+12^{|A|+1} possible choices of f∈ℬA​(P,γ)f\in{\mathcal{B}}_{A}(P,\gamma) such that they produce the monomial

𝐱|f​(σ−1​(1))|​𝐱|f​(σ−1​(2))|​…​𝐱|f​(σ−1​(n))|{\bf x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(1))|}{\bf x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(2))|}\dots{\bf x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(n))|}

such that

  1. (1)

    |f⁡(σ−1​(i))|=|f⁡(σ−1​(j))||f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|=|f(\sigma^{-1}(j))| if ii and jj are in the same block of [A][A].

  2. (2)

    |f⁡(σ−1​(i))|<|f⁡(σ−1​(j))||f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|<|f(\sigma^{-1}(j))| if ii is in a block of [A][A] to the left of the block containing jj.

Therefore,

∑f∈ℬA​(w,γ)∏i=1n𝐱|f​(σ−1​(i))|=2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ),\sum_{f\in\mathcal{B}_{A}(w,\gamma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{|f(\sigma^{-1}(i))|}=2^{|A|+1}{\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma)},

as desired. ∎

Corollary 6.5.

We have that 𝐊(w,γ,σ)=𝐊(w,γ′,σ)\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}=\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma^{\prime},\sigma)} if and only if Peak⁡(w,γ)=Peak⁡(w,γ′)\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)=\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma^{\prime}).

Given a peak set B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, define

𝐊(B,σ)=𝐊(w,γ,σ)\mathbf{K}_{(B,\sigma)}=\mathbf{K}_{(w,\gamma,\sigma)}

where (w,γ)(w,\gamma) is any labelled chain with Peak⁡(w,γ)=B\mathrm{Peak}(w,\gamma)=B.

7. Peak algebra in noncommuting variables and its dimension

Definition 7.1.

Let NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi be the space spanned by all enriched fundamental functions in noncommuting variables 𝐊(P,γ,σ){\mathbf{K}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}, or equivalently, the space spanned by the following set

{ℱ𝐆:𝐆​ is a labelled edge-coloured digraph}.\{{\mathscr{F}}_{\bf G}:{\bf G}\text{~is a labelled edge-coloured digraph}\}.

The space NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is called the peak algebra in noncommuting variables.

7.1. Enriched monomial functions

Given (B,σ)(B,\sigma) where B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, define the enriched monomial function in noncommuting variables 𝜼(B,σ){\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)} to be

𝜼(B,σ)=∑C⊆B(−1)|B|−|C|​𝐊(C,σ).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}=\sum_{C\subseteq B}(-1)^{|B|-|C|}\mathbf{K}_{(C,\sigma)}.

By inclusion-exclusion, we have

𝐊(B,σ)=∑C⊆B𝜼(C,σ).\mathbf{K}_{(B,\sigma)}=\sum_{C\subseteq B}{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(C,\sigma)}.
Corollary 7.2.

Both sets

{𝐊(B,σ): B⊆{2,3,…,n−1} is a peak set, σ∈𝔖n}\{{\mathbf{K}}_{(B,\sigma)}:\text{~$B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$ is a peak set, $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$}\}

and

{𝜼(B,σ): B⊆{2,3,…,n−1} is a peak set, σ∈𝔖n}\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}:\text{~$B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$ is a peak set, $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$}\}

span NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}.

Proof.

By definition NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is spanned by {𝐊(P,γ,σ)}\{{\mathbf{K}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}\}, and by Corollary 6.5, if Peak⁡(P,γ)=Peak⁡(P,γ′)\mathrm{Peak}(P,\gamma)=\mathrm{Peak}(P,\gamma^{\prime}), then 𝐊(P,γ,σ)=𝐊(P,γ′,σ){\mathbf{K}}_{(P,\gamma,\sigma)}={\mathbf{K}}_{(P,\gamma^{\prime},\sigma)}. Therefore, the set

{𝐊(B,σ): B⊆{2,3,…,n−1} is a peak set, σ∈𝔖n}\{{\mathbf{K}}_{(B,\sigma)}:\text{~$B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$ is a peak set, $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$}\}

spans NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}, and by triangulation we have

{𝜼(B,σ): B⊆{2,3,…,n−1} is a peak set, σ∈𝔖n}\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}:\text{~$B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$ is a peak set, $\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}$}\}

spans NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}.

∎

7.2. Enriched monomial functions to monomials

In order to show that the dimension of NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n} is the same as the number of odd set compositions of [n][n], we need the following lemma.

Lemma 7.3.

For any peak set B⊆[n−1]B\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we have

𝜼(B,σ)=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}.
Proof.

It follows from Proposition 6.4 that

𝜼(B,σ)\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)} =∑C⊆B(−1)|B|−|C|​∑A⊆[n−1]C⊆A∪(A+1)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ)\displaystyle=\sum_{C\subseteq B}(-1)^{|B|-|C|}\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]\atop C\subseteq A\cup(A+1)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}
=∑A⊆[n−1](∑C⊆(A∪(A+1))∩B(−1)|B|−|C|)​2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ)\displaystyle=\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]}\left(\sum_{C\subseteq(A\cup(A+1))\cap B}(-1)^{|B|-|C|}\right)2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}
=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1))2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).\displaystyle=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1))}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}.

The last equality follows from the observation that the sum inside the bracket vanishes unless (A∪(A+1))∩B=∅(A\cup(A+1))\cap B=\emptyset which is equivalent to A⊆[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1))A\subseteq[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1)). Note that Odd⁡(B)=[n−1]∖(B∪(B−1))\mathrm{Odd}(B)=[n-1]\setminus(B\cup(B-1)), thus

𝜼(B,σ)=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}.

∎

Lemma 7.4.

Let B⊆[n−1]B\subseteq[n-1] be a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Let σ′∈𝔖n\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. If

Std⁡(Odd⁡(B),σ)=Std⁡(Odd⁡(B),σ′),\mathrm{Std}(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma)=\mathrm{Std}(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma^{\prime}),

then

𝜼(B,σ)=𝜼(B,σ′).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}={\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma^{\prime})}.
Proof.

Note that

𝐌(Odd⁡(B),σ)=𝐌(Odd⁡(B),σ′).{\mathbf{M}}_{(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma)}={\mathbf{M}}_{(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma^{\prime})}.

Thus, for any A⊆Odd⁡(B)A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B),

𝐌(A,σ)=𝐌(A,σ′).{\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma)}={\mathbf{M}}_{(A,\sigma^{\prime})}.

Therefore,

𝜼(B,σ)=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ)=(−1)|B|​∑A⊆Odd⁡(B)2|A|+1​𝐌(A,σ′)=𝜼(B,σ′).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma)}=(-1)^{|B|}\sum_{A\subseteq\mathrm{Odd}(B)}2^{|A|+1}\mathbf{M}_{(A,\sigma^{\prime})}={\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma^{\prime})}.

∎

7.3. Bases of the peak algebra in noncommuting variables and its dimension

Recall that if B⊆[n−1]B\subseteq[n-1] is a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we say (B,σ)(B,\sigma) is enriched standard if (Odd⁡(B),σ)(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma) is standard.

Our main result of this section is the following.

Theorem 7.5.

The sets

{𝜼(B,σ):B⊆{2,3,…,n−1},σ∈𝔖n,(B,σ) is enriched standard}\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}:B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\},\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},(B,\sigma)\text{~is enriched standard}\}

and

{𝐊(B,σ):B⊆{2,3,…,n−1},σ∈𝔖n,(B,σ) is enriched standard}\{{\mathbf{K}}_{(B,\sigma)}:B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\},\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},(B,\sigma)\text{~is enriched standard}\}

are bases for NC​Πn.\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}. Moreover,

dim(NC​Πn)=|{ϕ⊨[n]:ϕ​ is odd}|.\dim(\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n})=|\{\phi\vDash[n]:\phi\text{~is odd}\}|.
Proof.

Given any pair (B,σ)(B,\sigma) where B⊆{2,3,…,n−1}B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\} is a peak set and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, let σ′\sigma^{\prime} be the unique permutation in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that

Std⁡(Odd⁡(B),σ)=(Odd⁡(B),σ′).\mathrm{Std}(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma)=(\mathrm{Odd}(B),\sigma^{\prime}).

By Lemma 7.4,

𝜼(B,σ)=𝜼(B,σ′).{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}={\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma^{\prime})}.

Moreover,

{𝜼(B,σ):B⊆{2,3,…,n−1},σ∈𝔖n,(B,σ) is enriched standard}\{{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}:B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\},\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},(B,\sigma)\text{~is enriched standard}\}

is linearly independent by triangularity of the transition matrix from 𝜼{\boldsymbol{\eta}} to 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}. Therefore, this set is a basis for NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}.

Observe that if (B,σ)(B,\sigma) is enriched standard, then for any C⊆BC\subseteq B, (C,σ)(C,\sigma) is also enriched standard. Therefore,

{𝐊(B,σ):B⊆{2,3,…,n−1},σ∈𝔖n,(B,σ) is enriched standard}\{{\mathbf{K}}_{(B,\sigma)}:B\subseteq\{2,3,\dots,n-1\},\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},(B,\sigma)\text{~is enriched standard}\}

also forms a basis for NC​Πn\mathrm{NC}\Pi_{n}. ∎

8. Hopf structure of the peak algebra in noncommuting variables

The goal of this section is to prove that NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is a Hopf subalgebra of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}.

Recall that the product in NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} is the regular product of power series. The coproduct in NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} is defined as follows (see [15]). By introducing another set of noncommuting variables 𝐲=𝐲1,𝐲2,…\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{y}_{1},\mathbf{y}_{2},\dots with linear order 𝐱1<𝐱2<⋯<𝐲1<𝐲2<⋯\mathbf{x}_{1}<\mathbf{x}_{2}<\cdots<\mathbf{y}_{1}<\mathbf{y}_{2}<\cdots, we have the following map composition

NCQSym⁡(𝐱)≅NCQSym⁡(𝐱,𝐲)→NCQSym(𝐱,𝐲)/∼→NCQSym⁡(𝐱)⊗NCQSym⁡(𝐲)f⁡(𝐱)↦f⁡(𝐱,𝐲)↦f¯​(𝐱,𝐲)↦∑f1¯​(𝐱)⊗f2¯​(𝐲)\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})&\cong&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})&\to&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})/\sim&\to&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{y})\\ f(\mathbf{x})&\mapsto&f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})&\mapsto&\bar{f}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})&\mapsto&\sum\bar{f_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\bar{f_{2}}(\mathbf{y})\end{array}

where ∼\sim denotes the relations 𝐱i​𝐲j=𝐲j​𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{y}_{j}=\mathbf{y}_{j}\mathbf{x}_{i} for all i,ji,j. Then, the coproduct is given by

Δ:NCQSym⁡(𝐱)→NCQSym⁡(𝐱)⊗NCQSym⁡(𝐲)≅NCQSym⁡(𝐱)⊗NCQSym⁡(𝐱)f⁡(𝐱)↦∑f1¯​(𝐱)⊗f2¯​(𝐲)↦∑f1¯​(𝐱)⊗f2¯​(𝐱)\begin{array}[]{cccccc}\Delta:&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})&\to&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{y})&\cong&\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\mathrm{NCQSym}(\mathbf{x})\\ &f(\mathbf{x})&\mapsto&\sum\bar{f_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\bar{f_{2}}(\mathbf{y})&\mapsto&\sum\bar{f_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\otimes\bar{f_{2}}(\mathbf{x})\end{array}

Let 𝐆\bf G be a labelled edge-coloured digraph, and let nn be a positive integer. Then 𝐆+n{\bf G}+n is the labelled edge-coloured digraph obtained by replacing each vertex aa of 𝐆\bf G by a+na+n.

Given labelled edge-coloured digraphs 𝐆{\bf G} and 𝐇{\bf H}, by [5, Proposition 10.1]

𝒴𝐆​𝒴𝐇=𝒴𝐆|𝐇{\mathscr{Y}}_{\bf G}{\mathscr{Y}}_{\bf H}={\mathscr{Y}}_{{\bf G}|{\bf H}}

where 𝐆|𝐇{\bf G}|{\bf H} is the digraph of disjoint union of 𝐆{\bf G} and 𝐇+|V⁡(𝐆)|{\bf H}+|V({\bf G})|.

Let 𝐆\bf G be a labelled edge-coloured digraph. The standardization of 𝐆\bf G, denoted Std⁡(𝐆)\mathrm{Std}({\bf G}), is the labelled edge-coloured digraph obtained by replacing the iith smallest element of V⁡(𝐆)V({\bf G}) by ii. For a subset AA of V⁡(𝐆)V({\bf G}), let 𝐆|A{\bf G}|_{A} be the induced labelled edge-coloured subdigraph of 𝐆{\bf G} with vertex set AA. An edge-coloured subdigraph 𝐅{\bf F} of 𝐆{\bf G} is called a {→,⇒}\{\rightarrow,\Rightarrow\}-induced subdigraph of 𝐆{\bf G} if 𝐅{\bf F} is an induced subdigraph of 𝐆{\bf G} and if a∈V⁡(𝐅)a\in V({\bf F}) and either a→ba\rightarrow b or a⇒ba\Rightarrow b in 𝐆{\bf G}, then b∈V⁡(𝐅)b\in V({\bf F}). Then by [5, Proposition 10.2]

Δ⁡(𝒴𝐆)=∑𝐅𝒴Std⁡(𝐆|V⁡(𝐆)∖V⁡(𝐅))⊗𝒴Std⁡(𝐅)\Delta({\mathscr{Y}}_{\bf G})=\sum_{{\bf F}}{\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathrm{Std}({\bf G}|_{V({\bf G})\setminus V({\bf F})})}\otimes{\mathscr{Y}}_{\mathrm{Std}({\bf F})}

where the sum is over all {→,⇒}\{\rightarrow,\Rightarrow\}-induced subdigraphs 𝐅{\bf F} of 𝐆{\bf G}.

With a similar proof for the product and coproduct of enriched generalized chromatic functions. We have

ℱ𝐆​ℱ𝐇=ℱ𝐆|𝐇,{\mathscr{F}}_{\bf G}{\mathscr{F}}_{\bf H}={\mathscr{F}}_{{\bf G}|{\bf H}},

and

Δ⁡(ℱ𝐆)=∑𝐅ℱStd⁡(𝐆|V⁡(𝐆)∖V⁡(𝐅))⊗ℱStd⁡(𝐅)\Delta({\mathscr{F}}_{\bf G})=\sum_{{\bf F}}{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathrm{Std}({\bf G}|_{V({\bf G})\setminus V({\bf F})})}\otimes{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathrm{Std}({\bf F})}

where the sum is over all {→,⇒}\{\rightarrow,\Rightarrow\}-induced subdigraphs 𝐅{\bf F} of 𝐆{\bf G}.

Therefore NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi is isomorphic to a Hopf subalgebra of NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym}.

9. The labelled descent-to-peak map

The labelled descent-to-peak map from NCQSym\mathrm{NCQSym} to NC​Π\mathrm{NC}\Pi, denoted ΘNCQSym\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}, is the linear map

(9.1) ΘNCQSym:NCQSym→NC​Π𝐅(A,σ)↦𝐊(A∖((A+1)∪{1}),σ)\begin{array}[]{cccc}\Theta_{\mathrm{NCQSym}}:&\mathrm{NCQSym}&\to&\mathrm{NC}\Pi\\ &\mathbf{F}_{(A,\sigma)}&\mapsto&\mathbf{K}_{(A\setminus((A+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}\end{array}

for all standard pairs (A,σ)(A,\sigma).

Let A={a1<a2<⋯<ak}⊆[n−1]A=\{a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots<a_{k}\}\subseteq[n-1] with n−akn-a_{k} is odd. We define

ODiff(A)={ai:1≤i≤k,ai−ai−1 is odd}\mathrm{ODiff}(A)=\{a_{i}:1\leq i\leq k,a_{i}-a_{i-1}\text{ is odd}\}

where a0=0a_{0}=0. For example, if A={1,3,4,8}⊆[9]A=\{1,3,4,8\}\subseteq[9], then ODiff⁡(A)={1,4}\mathrm{ODiff}(A)=\{1,4\}.

Remark that ODiff⁡(A)\mathrm{ODiff}(A) is an odd set, and there is a unique peak set BB such that

Odd⁡(B)=ODiff⁡(A).\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\mathrm{ODiff}(A).

The following lemma will be useful in the study of the labelled descent-to-peak map.

Lemma 9.1.

Let A⊆[n−1]A\subseteq[n-1] and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Then

∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](−1)|C|​𝐊(C∖((C+1)∪{1}),σ)={(−1)n−1−|B|​𝜼(B,σ) if ​n−max⁡(A)​ is odd,0 otherwise,\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}(-1)^{|C|}\mathbf{K}_{(C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}=\begin{cases}(-1)^{n-1-|B|}{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}&\text{ if }n-\max(A)\text{ is odd,}\\ 0&\text{ otherwise,}\end{cases}

where BB is the unique peak set such that Odd⁡(B)=ODiff⁡(A)\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\mathrm{ODiff}(A).

Proof.

Consider the set {C⊆[n−1]:A⊆C}\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A\subseteq C\}. Let the sign of CC to be (−1)|C|(-1)^{|C|}.

We first show that if n−max⁡(A)n-\max(A) is even, then

∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](−1)|C|​𝐊(C∖((C+1)∪{1}),σ)=0\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}(-1)^{|C|}\mathbf{K}_{(C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}=0

using a sign reversing involution ı\imath with no fixed point defined as follows.

Let C≥max⁡(A)C_{\geq\max(A)} be the set of the elements of CC that are bigger than or equal to max⁡(A)\max(A). Let

(C≥max⁡(A)∖{1})∪{max(A),n+1}={max(A)=d1<d2<⋯<dk=n+1}.(C_{\geq\max(A)}\setminus\{1\})\cup\{\max(A),n+1\}=\{\max(A)=d_{1}<d_{2}<\cdots<d_{k}=n+1\}.

The set {1≤i≤k−1:di+1−di​ is odd}\{1\leq i\leq k-1:d_{i+1}-d_{i}\text{~is odd}\} is non-empty since dk−d1=n+1−max⁡(A)d_{k}-d_{1}=n+1-\max(A) is odd. Let j=min⁡({1≤i≤k−1:di+1−di​ is odd})j=\min(\{1\leq i\leq k-1:d_{i+1}-d_{i}\text{~is odd}\}); that is jj is the smallest integer such that dj+1−djd_{j+1}-d_{j} is odd. If C∩{dj+1,dj+2,…,dj+1}=∅C\cap\{d_{j}+1,d_{j}+2,\dots,d_{j+1}\}=\emptyset, set mC=0m_{C}=0, otherwise, let mCm_{C} be the largest integer such that

dj+1,dj+2,…,dj+mC∈C∩{dj+1,dj+2,…,dj+1}.d_{j}+1,d_{j}+2,\ldots,d_{j}+m_{C}\in C\cap\{d_{j}+1,d_{j}+2,\dots,d_{j+1}\}.

Now define

ı:{C⊆[n−1]:A⊆C}→{C⊆[n−1]:A⊆C}C↦{C∖{dj+mC}if ​mC​ is odd,C∪{dj+mC+1}if ​mC​ is even.\begin{array}[]{cccc}\imath:&\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A\subseteq C\}&\rightarrow&\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A\subseteq C\}\\ &C&\mapsto&\begin{cases}C\setminus\{d_{j}+m_{C}\}&\text{if ~}m_{C}\text{~is odd,}\\ C\cup\{d_{j}+m_{C}+1\}&\text{if ~}m_{C}\text{~is even.}\end{cases}\end{array}

Then ı\imath is a sign reversing involution with no fixed point. Moreover, for any CC, we have

ı⁡(C)∖((ı⁡(C)+1)∪{1})=C∖((C+1)∪{1}),\imath(C)\setminus((\imath(C)+1)\cup\{1\})=C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),

and so

𝐊(C∖((C+1)∪{1}),σ)=𝐊OPENı⁡(C)∖((ı⁡(C)+1)∪{1}),σ).\mathbf{K}_{(C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}=\mathbf{K}_{\imath(C)\setminus((\imath(C)+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}.

Consequently,

∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](−1)|C|​𝐊(C∖((C+1)∪{1}),σ)=0.\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}(-1)^{|C|}\mathbf{K}_{(C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}=0.

Let n−max⁡(A)n-\max(A) be odd and let BB be the unique peak set such that Odd⁡(B)=ODiff⁡(A)\mathrm{Odd}(B)=\mathrm{ODiff}(A). We want to show that

∑A⊆C⊆[n−1](−1)|C|​𝐊(C∖((C+1)∪{1}),σ)=(−1)n−1−|B|​𝜼(B,σ)\sum_{A\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]}(-1)^{|C|}\mathbf{K}_{(C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}),\sigma)}=(-1)^{n-1-|B|}{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{(B,\sigma)}

using a sing reversing involution ȷ\jmath defined as follows.

Define

ȷ:{C⊆[n−1]:A⊆C}→{C⊆[n−1]:A⊆C}C↦{Cif ​B⊆C,C∖{(min⁡(B)∖C)−1}if B⊈C,(min(B)∖C)−1∈C,C∪{(min⁡(B)∖C)−1}if B⊈C,(min(B)∖C)−1∉C.\begin{array}[]{cccc}\jmath:&\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A\subseteq C\}&\rightarrow&\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A\subseteq C\}\\ &C&\mapsto&\begin{cases}C&\text{if~}B\subseteq C,\\ C\setminus\{\ (\min(B)\setminus C)-1\}&\text{if~}B\not\subseteq C,(\min(B)\setminus C)-1\in C,\\ C\cup\{\ (\min(B)\setminus C)-1\}&\text{if~}B\not\subseteq C,(\min(B)\setminus C)-1\not\in C.\\ \end{cases}\end{array}

Note that the set of fixed points of ȷ\jmath is

{C⊆[n−1]:A,B⊆C}.\{C\subseteq[n-1]:A,B\subseteq C\}.

We have that

{C∖((C+1)∪{1}):A,B⊆C⊆[n−1]}={D:D⊆B}.\{C\setminus((C+1)\cup\{1\}):A,B\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1]\}=\{D:D\subseteq B\}.

The reason for this equality is that if A,B⊆C⊆[n−1]A,B\subseteq C\subseteq[n-1], then

In this section, we study the relation between the functions that satisfy the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equation and the elements of the peak algebra in noncommuting variables.

In this section we define the space of Schur QQ-functions in noncommuting variables, which is a Hopf subalgebra of symmetric functions in noncommuting variables NCSym\mathrm{NCSym}. We will follow notation from [36].

11.1. Symmetric functions in noncommuting variables

𝐪π=∑τ≤πτ​ is odd set partition|μ⁡(0^,τ)|​2ℓ⁡(τ)​𝐩τ.\mathbf{q}_{\pi}=\sum_{\tau\leq\pi\atop\tau\text{ is odd set partition}}|\mu(\hat{0},\tau)|2^{\ell(\tau)}\mathbf{p}_{\tau}.
